# Actual simplex facet data and a sharp obstruction to rowwise vertex splitting

This note gives identities for arbitrary simplex cut incidences. It does not
prove or refute the joint-row inequality for all such incidences. It does
refute a denominator-preserving reduction obtained by positively splitting
each cut direction into vertex-isolating directions at the same source.

## 1. A shared-facet stochastic matrix

Let (K=\operatorname{conv}(P_0,\ldots,P_d)\subset\mathbb R^d) be a
nondegenerate simplex of volume (k), let (y\in\operatorname{int}K),
and let (v_0,\ldots,v_d\) be a spanning balanced normal circuit:

\[
v_i\ne0,\qquad \sum_i v_i=0.
\]

The closed caps are (H_i=\{x:v_i\cdot(x-y)\ge0\}). Set

\[
t_{ij}=v_i\cdot(P_j-y),\quad
Q_i=\frac{|K\cap H_i|}{k},\quad
S_i=\frac{\mathcal H_{d-1}(K\cap\partial H_i)}{k\|v_i\|}.
\]

Every cap is proper, with (0<Q_i<1) and (S_i>0). For the facet
opposite (P_j), let (F_{ij}\in[0,1]) denote its captured fraction
with its ordinary ((d-1))-dimensional measure. Then

\[
F_{ij}=Q_i-\frac{t_{ij}}dS_i.
\tag{1}
\]

To prove (1), apply the divergence theorem to (x\mapsto x-P_j)
on the cap. On facets containing (P_j) the normal flux is zero.
On the opposite facet its full flux is (dk), so its captured part
contributes (dkF_{ij}). On the new cut face, the outward normal is

\(-v_i/\|v_i\|\), and the flux is (t_{ij}/\|v_i\|\).

The total flux is therefore (dkF_{ij}+t_{ij}kS_i=dkQ_i).
Facet intersections and edges have no relevant surface measure, so the
argument includes cuts through vertices or edges. The same proof in
dimension one uses counting measure on the two endpoint facets.

Put

\[
M=\sum_i Q_i/S_i>0,\qquad
X_{ij}=\frac{F_{ij}}{S_iM}.
\tag{2}
\]

The matrix (X\) is nonnegative and each column sums to one:

\[
\sum_iX_{ij}=1-\frac{\sum_i t_{ij}}{dM}=1.
\tag{3}
\]

If \(\lambda_j>0\) are the source barycentric coordinates, then

\[
a_i:=\sum_j\lambda_jX_{ij}=\frac{Q_i}{S_iM},
\qquad \sum_i a_i=1,
\qquad t_{ij}=dM(a_i-X_{ij}).
\tag{4}
\]

Consequently the actual joint-row input is

\[
f_i=\frac{d a_i}{Q_i^{1/d}}.
\tag{5}
\]

Unlike the isolated-vertex matrix, an arbitrary row may have no zero
entry. Its entries are the actual cap fractions on the SAME (d+1)
facets, divided by the row's coarea normalization. Thus merely keeping
column stochasticity discards additional shared-facet geometry.

## 2. The exact minimum normalization cost of splitting one direction

Fix one nonzero direction (v) through (y), and write its signed vertex
values as (t_j=v\cdot(P_j-y)). Consider any finite decomposition

\[
v=\sum_{r=1}^N v^{(r)},
\tag{6}
\]

where each (v^{(r)}\) has exactly one positive signed vertex value

\(h_r>0\), and all its other vertex values are nonpositive.
Positive coefficients in a decomposition can be absorbed into the
normals, so (6) includes positive mixtures of directions.

For every component, the cut piece is a pyramid from its unique positive
vertex, and hence

\[
\frac{Q^{(r)}}{S^{(r)}}=\frac{h_r}{d}.
\]

The positive-part triangle inequality at each vertex gives

\[
\sum_r \frac{Q^{(r)}}{S^{(r)}}
=\frac1d\sum_rh_r
\ge\frac1d\sum_j(t_j)_+.
\tag{7}
\]

This bound is attained when zero vertex values are allowed. Let
\(I=\{i:t_i>0\}\) and
\(P=\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i t_i>0\).
For each (i\in I), assign a component with vertex values

\[
t^{(i)}_i=t_i,\qquad
t^{(i)}_j=\frac{\lambda_i t_i}{P}t_j\quad(t_j<0),
\qquad t^{(i)}_j=0\quad(j\ne i, t_j\ge0).
\tag{8}
\]

Each such vector has barycentric mean zero, so it is the vertex-value
vector of a unique affine functional vanishing at (y). Their sum is
the original vector. Every component has exactly one positive vertex,
and their heights sum to \(\sum(t_j)_+\). This proves the asserted
minimum. Requiring strictly negative values at the remaining vertices
cannot lower (7).

The original cap's ratio (Q/S) need not equal or exceed this minimum.
The next section gives a strict, rational example.

## 3. Exact two-versus-two formula and a genuine circuit obstruction

For a tetrahedral cap with margins ((p,q,-r,-s)), all four parameters
positive, set

\[
N=pq(r+s)+rs(p+q).
\]

The exact cap and coarea formulas, obtained by triangulating the
quadrilateral section, are

\[
\alpha=\frac{ps}{(p+r)(p+s)(q+s)},\quad
\delta=\frac{qr}{(p+r)(q+s)(q+r)},
\]
\[
Q=p(\alpha+\delta)+\frac{q^2}{(q+s)(q+r)},\qquad
S=3(\alpha+\delta).
\]

They simplify to the exact normalization deficit

\[
\frac{p+q}{3}-\frac QS
=\frac{pq(rs-pq)}{3N}.
\tag{9}
\]

Use the standard tetrahedron (operatorname{conv}(0,e_1,e_2,e_3)),
whose volume is (1/6), and source

\[
y=(1/6,1/6,1/6),\qquad
\lambda=(1/2,1/6,1/6,1/6).
\]

Choose the four actual balanced normals

\[
v_0=(-1,-5,-6),\quad v_1=(1,0,0),\quad
v_2=(0,5,0),\quad v_3=(0,0,6).
\tag{10}
\]

They sum to zero and have rank three, so their unique dependence is
positive and minimal. The first cap has margins ((2,1,-3,-4)), and

\[
Q_0=13/60,\quad S_0=1/4,\quad Q_0/S_0=13/15.
\]

The other three caps each have fraction (125/216), with normalized
coarea measures (25/12,5/12,25/72), respectively. Thus the actual
full-circuit normalization is (M=21/5).

However, (7) says that EVERY positive decomposition of (v_0) into
vertex-isolating normals through this source has total normalization
at least one. Hence replacing that row while retaining the other rows
increases (M) by at least (2/15). This is a strict exact obstruction
to any denominator-preserving or denominator-decreasing row-splitting
argument.

The minimum is attained by the two margin vectors

\[
(2,0,-18/7,-24/7),\qquad(0,1,-3/7,-4/7),
\]

which both have zero source barycentric mean and sum to the original
row. Their unique positive heights are two and one.

## 4. What remains unavailable

The construction does not rule out a coupled convex-mixture theorem
for complete (f)-vectors. Such a theorem would have to account for
the increase in (M), possible merging of pieces assigned to the same
vertex, and the shared facet fractions (F_{ij}). Rowwise linearity of
the normals alone supplies none of those comparisons.

No convex-mixture representation with these properties is proved here.
The unrestricted simplex joint-row assertion remains unresolved by
this argument. In particular neither the obstruction nor a finite
falsification screen is a counterexample to that assertion or to OC.
